module_title: Drainage and Wastewater Piping with PVC

lessons.title: Understanding Drain, Waste, and Vent (DWV) Systems
lessons.body:
A DWV system has three jobs: drain wastewater away, carry solid waste to a sewer or septic tank, and vent sewer gases safely outside. In a typical African home, PVC pipes are used because they are cheap, smooth inside (so waste flows easily), and resist corrosion. The drain pipes slope downward so gravity does the work. Waste pipes carry toilets, sinks, and showers. Vent pipes go up through the roof and let air in, so water flows smoothly and gases escape. Without a vent, a toilet flush can suck the water out of a nearby sink trap, letting sewer smell into the house.

Start by mapping your system. Use a pencil and paper to sketch where the toilet, sinks, showers, and outside tank or sewer line are. Mark the main stack (the big vertical pipe) and where it exits the building. In most homes, the main stack is 110 mm PVC for the toilet, and branch lines are 50 mm or 40 mm for sinks and showers. Every fixture needs a trap (P-trap or bottle trap) to hold water and block gas. The vent pipe is usually 50 mm and must go above the roof by at least 300 mm. If you cannot vent through the roof, an air admittance valve (AAV) can work, but check local rules.

When installing, cut PVC with a fine-tooth saw or pipe cutter. Deburr the cut with a file or sandpaper. Dry-fit everything first. Use PVC solvent cement: apply primer to both pipe and fitting, then cement, push together with a quarter turn, and hold for 30 seconds. Slope horizontal drain pipes at least 1:60 (about 1 cm per 60 cm) and no more than 1:40 (1.5 cm per 40 cm). Too little slope causes clogs; too much slope lets water run away and leave solids behind. Support pipes every 1.2 m with plastic clips or straps. Test by pouring 20 litres of water down each fixture and checking for leaks. Vent pipes must be clear and open to air. Never connect a vent to a chimney or use a vent as a drain. Keep it simple, slope it right, and vent it well.

lessons.title: Selecting the Right Pipe Diameter for Toilets, Sinks, and Showers
lessons.body:
Using the wrong pipe diameter is a top cause of clogs and slow drains. In PVC DWV systems, the size is measured by the outside diameter (OD) but named by nominal bore: 40 mm, 50 mm, 75 mm, 110 mm. For a toilet, you need 110 mm (4-inch) pipe. A toilet discharges about 6â9 litres per flush with solid waste. A smaller pipe will block. The toilet's waste outlet is usually 100 mm or 110 mm, so the pipe must match. Never reduce below 110 mm for a toilet branch.

For sinks (kitchen and bathroom), use 40 mm (1.5-inch) pipe. That handles soapy water and small food particles. If the sink is far from the main stack (more than 3 metres), use 50 mm to reduce clogging. For showers and bathtubs, use 40 mm or 50 mm. A shower drain sees hair and soap scum; 50 mm is safer if multiple fixtures share the line. For floor drains (common in wet rooms), use 50 mm. For a washing machine, use 50 mm because it pumps water fast.

When combining fixtures, the branch pipe must be large enough for the total flow. A bathroom group (toilet, sink, shower) often uses a 110 mm branch for the toilet and 50 mm branches for sink and shower, all connecting to a 110 mm main stack. The main stack should be 110 mm for a single-storey house. For two storeys, keep 110 mm if only one toilet per stack; otherwise use 110 mm and add a second stack. The pipe from the house to the septic tank or sewer (the drain line) should be 110 mm minimum. If the run is longer than 15 metres or has multiple toilets, use 160 mm. Always check local plumbing codes. In many African countries, 110 mm PVC is standard for main drains. Use fittings (bends, tees, wyes) of the same diameter. Avoid reducing diameter in the direction of flow. A 110 mm toilet branch must never connect to a 50 mm line. If you are unsure, go one size largerâit costs a little more but prevents blockages.

lessons.title: Proper Slope for Drainage Pipes (1:60 to 1:40)
lessons.body:
Slope, or fall, is the angle at which a drain pipe drops. If the pipe is too flat, water moves slowly and solids settle, causing clogs. If it is too steep, water runs away too fast, leaving solids behind. The correct slope for PVC drainage pipes is between 1:60 and 1:40. That means for every 60 units of horizontal run, the pipe drops 1 unit (1:60), up to 1 unit per 40 units (1:40). In practical terms: 1 cm drop per 60 cm length (minimum) to 1.5 cm drop per 40 cm length (maximum). For a 5-metre run, the total drop should be between 8.3 cm (at 1:60) and 12.5 cm (at 1:40).

To set the slope, use a spirit level and a measuring tape. Mark the start and end heights. For example, if the drain starts at the toilet and runs 5 metres to the septic tank, the end should be 8â12 cm lower. You can use a line level or a string line with a line level. A simpler method: use a 1-metre level. For 1:60, the bubble should show a drop of about 1.7 cm per metre (since 100 cm / 60 = 1.67 cm). For 1:40, drop 2.5 cm per metre. Mark the pipe supports accordingly. Support the pipe every 1.2 m so it does not sag. Sagging creates a belly where water and waste collect.

In Africa, many homes have sandy or clay soils. Dig the trench with a slight slope, then compact the bottom. Lay a 50 mm bed of sand or fine gravel to protect the pipe. After installing, check slope with a level before gluing. If the pipe is already glued, you can adjust supports. Never slope a drain pipe backwards. For vent pipes, slope does not matter; they go up. For horizontal vent pipes (if any), slope back to the drain at 1:60. Test by pouring a bucket of water at the high end; it should flow smoothly out the low end without gurgling. If it pools, adjust slope. Remember: 1:60 is minimum, 1:40 is maximum. Aim for 1:50 as a good middle. Write the numbers on your hand: 1 cm per 60 cm, 1.5 cm per 40 cm.

lessons.title: Installing P-Traps and Vent Pipes to Prevent Sewer Gas
lessons.body:
Sewer gas smells like rotten eggs and can be dangerous. It comes from decomposing waste in the drain, septic tank, or sewer. To keep it out of your home, every fixture needs a trap, and the system needs a vent. A P-trap is a U-shaped pipe that holds water. That water seal blocks gas. The trap must have a water depth of 50â100 mm. Too shallow, and it evaporates quickly; too deep, and it slows flow. For sinks and showers, use a 40 mm or 50 mm P-trap. For toilets, the toilet itself has a built-in trap. Never install a trap with a flexible corrugated pipeâit catches debris and smells. Use smooth PVC.

Install the P-trap directly under the fixture. The trap arm (the pipe from the trap to the drain line) must slope at 1:60 to 1:40 and be no more than 1.5 m long for 40 mm pipe, or 1.8 m for 50 mm. If the trap arm is too long, the trap can siphon dry. After the trap, connect to a vent pipe. The vent must rise vertically (or at 45 degrees) to at least 300 mm above the roof. It should be at least 50 mm diameter. If you cannot go through the roof, use an air admittance valve (AAV) on the trap arm, but AAVs can fail; check local rules. In many African homes, a single 50 mm vent stack for the whole house works if it is correctly sized.

Vent pipes must be clear. Do not stuff them with insulation or let birds nest in them. Cover the top with a vent cap or mesh. For a bathroom group, you can use a common vent: a 50 mm pipe that connects the sink and shower traps and goes up. The toilet is vented through the main stack. When gluing, use PVC primer and cement. Support the vent pipe every 1.2 m. Test the system: run water in all fixtures, then smell near the traps. If you smell gas, check for a dry trap or a blocked vent. Pour a cup of water into floor drains every week to keep the trap seal. In dry season, traps can evaporate; add cooking oil to slow evaporation. Never connect a vent to a chimney or use a drain as a vent. Keep vents separate and open to air.

lessons.title: Connecting to Existing Septic Tanks or Municipal Sewers
lessons.body:
Before you connect, know where your waste goes. In many African cities, you connect to a municipal sewer line in the street. In rural or peri-urban areas, you connect to a septic tank and soakaway. Never connect stormwater to a septic tank or sewerâit overloads the system. First, locate the existing pipe or tank. For a septic tank, the inlet pipe is usually 110 mm PVC. For a sewer, the connection point is a Y-junction or a manhole. If you are unsure, ask neighbours or the local council. You need permission to dig up a public road or connect to a municipal sewer. In some areas, you must hire a licensed plumber.

For a septic tank, run a 110 mm PVC pipe from the house to the tank inlet. Slope at 1:60 to 1:40. The pipe should be laid on a 50 mm sand bed, with sand around it. Do not use 90-degree elbows; use two 45-degree bends or a long-sweep bend to reduce clogging. At the tank, the inlet should be at least 50 mm above the water level. Seal the pipe into the tank wall with mortar or a rubber grommet. If the tank is far (over 15 m), use 160 mm pipe. For a municipal sewer, connect to the existing line via a Y-junction or a saddle. The connection must be watertight. Use a rubber coupling or a PVC adaptor. Never reduce pipe size at the connection. The pipe from the house to the sewer should be 110 mm minimum. If the sewer is deeper than 1.2 m, you may need a drop manhole to avoid a steep slope.

After connecting, test by flushing toilets and running water. Check for leaks at joints. If you connect to a sewer, install a backwater valve if the sewer can flood. In many African cities, sewers overflow during heavy rain. A backwater valve prevents sewage from entering your home. For septic tanks, pump out the tank every 2â3 years. Never pour chemicals that kill bacteriaâthey stop the tank from working. If you connect to a sewer, do not dump cooking oil or sanitary pads; they cause blockages. Keep a cleanout every 15 m on long runs. A cleanout is a Y-fitting with a screw cap that lets you rod the line. Label your pipes: 'SEWER' or 'SEPTIC'. If you sell the house, the next owner will thank you.

lessons.title: Common Drainage Problems in African Homes and How to Fix Them
lessons.body:
Slow drains are the most common problem. Usually, it is a clog of hair, soap, food, or toilet paper. First, try a plunger. If that fails, use a drain snake (manual or drill-powered). For sinks, remove the P-trap and clean it. For toilets, use a toilet auger. Never use caustic soda on PVCâit can soften the pipe. Instead, use a mixture of baking soda and vinegar, then flush with hot water. If the clog is in the main line, open the cleanout and rod it. In many African homes, tree roots enter pipes through joints. If you suspect roots, call a plumber with a camera. You may need to replace that section with new PVC and seal joints well.

Bad smells mean a dry trap or a blocked vent. Pour a litre of water into floor drains and unused sinks. If the smell persists, check the vent on the roof. Birds, leaves, or a dead rat can block it. Clear the vent with a plumber's snake. If you have an air admittance valve, replace it. Another cause: a broken pipe under the floor. Look for wet patches or extra green grass. Fix by cutting out the damaged section and coupling a new piece with rubber couplings or PVC cement. Gurgling sounds mean the vent is partially blocked or the pipe is undersized. Check that the vent is at least 50 mm and goes above the roof. If you have a septic tank, gurgling can mean the tank is full. Pump it out.

Frequent clogs in toilets often mean the pipe is too small or slope is wrong. Toilets need 110 mm pipe. If you have 50 mm, replace it. Slope must be 1:60 to 1:40. If the pipe is too flat, water runs slow. If too steep, solids stay behind. Fix by re-laying the pipe with correct slope. Another problem: roots and soil settlement. In sandy soil, pipes can shift. Use flexible couplings or add supports. In clay soil, pipes can crack. Replace cracked pipes. For floor drains that overflow, the trap may be clogged. Remove the grate and clean. If you have a septic tank, do not use too much bleach or antibacterial soapâit kills the bacteria. Add a bucket of water to the tank monthly to keep it active. For municipal sewers, if your neighbours have backups, the main sewer is blocked. Report to the council. Never open a manhole yourself; it is dangerous. Keep a basic toolkit: plunger, drain snake, bucket, gloves, and a torch. Most problems are preventable with correct installation and monthly maintenance.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Drainage & Wastewater Piping with PVC

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in the Drainage and Wastewater Piping with PVC module into a single job-site companion. It is written for the African plumber, hardware retailer, small contractor, and property developer who needs to install, price, and troubleshoot PVC drainage systems that work the first time â in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Kampala, Dar es Salaam, or Johannesburg. Every specification below is tied to a recognised standard so you can quote it to a client, a building inspector, or a supplier and defend your price.

Why this matters commercially: drainage failures are the single most expensive plumbing defect in African residential construction. A wrongly sloped 110 mm line can cost a landlord a tenant, a contractor a retention payment, and a retailer a warranty claim. Getting slope, diameter, and venting right on day one protects your margin.

1. Drain, Waste and Vent (DWV) â the three jobs in one system

A DWV system does three things at once, and every design decision serves all three:

  • Drain â carry soiled water away from the fixture by gravity.
  • Waste â transport solids and greywater through the pipe without blocking.
  • Vent â admit air behind the flow so traps are not siphoned dry, and release sewer gas above the roof.

In African low-rise housing, the most common mistake is treating the vent as optional. Without a vent, a WC flush pulls the water out of a nearby basin P-trap, and the bathroom smells of sewer gas within weeks. A vent stack costs very little at construction stage and is extremely expensive to retrofit.

2. Selecting the right pipe diameter

Undersized pipe blocks; oversized pipe deposits solids because flow velocity drops. Use the standard fixture-unit (FU) method and match it to locally available PVC sizes (40, 50, 75, 110, 160 mm).

Table 1 â Minimum PVC drain sizes and fixture units (FU) for common African domestic fixtures
Fixture / applianceMinimum trap & branch (mm)Fixture units (FU)Notes
WC (water closet, 6â9 L flush)1104â6Never reduce below 110 mm on the branch or the WC pan outlet
Wash basin / hand wash40 (32 min.)150 mm gives better self-cleansing on long runs
Shower / bath502Use 50 mm waste with a 50 mm P-trap
Kitchen sink (domestic)502Fit a grease trap before the drain in commercial kitchens
Washing machine (domestic)502â3Standpipe must be 600â900 mm high to prevent backflow
Floor gully / yard drain752Fit a gully trap, not a plain open pipe
Main horizontal drain, 1â3 dwellings110Up to ~20 FUIncrease to 160 mm above ~20 FU or on runs over 15 m

Source: Fixture-unit values consolidated from BS EN 12056-2:2000 (BSI) and the Uniform Plumbing Code Table 702.1 (IAPMO). Diameters reflect the metric PVC range commonly stocked in East and West African markets (e.g. Kenpoly, Duraplast, Interplast).

3. Proper slope: 1:60 to 1:40

Slope (fall) is the single biggest determinant of whether a drain self-cleanses or silts up. For 110 mm PVC soil and waste pipes, the practical working range is 1:60 to 1:40 â that is, 16.7 mm to 25 mm of fall per metre of pipe.

  • Too flat (<1:60): velocity is too low, solids settle, and you get recurring blockages and smells.
  • Too steep (>1:40 on long runs): liquids outrun solids, leaving the solids behind, and traps can self-siphon.
  • Sweet spot: aim for 1:50 (20 mm/m) as a default target, which sits comfortably inside the 1:60â1:40 band and is easy to set with a spirit level and a 20 mm packer.
Table 2 â Fall per metre and per 5 m pipe length at common gradients
GradientFall per 1 mFall per 5 m lengthTypical use
1:6016.7 mm83 mmMinimum acceptable for 110 mm main drains
1:50 (recommended)20 mm100 mmDefault for 110 mm soil & waste runs
1:4025 mm125 mmMaximum sensible fall on long 110 mm runs
1:30 or steeper33 mm+167 mm+Short branch wastes only (e.g. basin to stack)

Source: Gradients consistent with BS EN 12056-2:2000 Annex B and South African National Building Regulations Part P (Drainage), which together set the 1:60â1:40 working band for 110 mm PVC soil and waste pipes.

4. P-traps and vent pipes: stopping sewer gas

The P-trap holds a water seal (typically 50â75 mm deep) that blocks sewer gas. The vent protects that seal from being siphoned away when a large volume â usually a WC flush â passes down the stack. Three rules that save callbacks:

  1. One trap per fixture. Never double-trap; it causes slow drainage and gurgling.
  2. Vent within 1.5 m of the trap (or as close as local code allows) so the branch is protected.
  3. Vent stack must terminate in open air, at least 150 mm above the roof and away from windows and air intakes â critical in dense African compounds where buildings sit close together.

â  SAFETY WARNING â SEWER GAS AND CONFINED SPACES

Sewer gas contains hydrogen sulphide (HâS), methane and, in some systems, carbon monoxide. It is toxic, explosive in confined spaces and can cause loss of consciousness within minutes at high concentrations. Never enter a septic tank, soakaway, manhole or inspection chamber without forced ventilation, a calibrated multi-gas detector, a harness and a standby person at the surface. Never use an open flame to test for gas leaks. If you smell HâS (rotten eggs) indoors, ventilate immediately, isolate the affected trap, and find the dry trap or broken seal before re-occupying the space. In many African jurisdictions, confined-space entry is a statutory permit-to-work activity â check your national OSH authority (e.g. DOSHS in Kenya, NECA in Nigeria) before entering.

5. Connecting to septic tanks or municipal sewers

Confirm the receiving point before you order pipe â this is where budgets blow out. Ask four questions:

  • Is there a municipal sewer? If yes, get the invert level and connection point from the utility (e.g. Nairobi Water, Lagos Water Corporation, GWCL). Municipal connections may require an inspection chamber and a paid permit.
  • If septic: size the tank for at least 2 days' retention; provide a separate soakaway or drainage field sized to local soil percolation.
  • Invert levels: the drain must fall continuously to the tank/sewer. If the sewer is higher than your site, you need a pumped chamber â price this into the quote early.
  • Access: install an inspection chamber or rodding eye at every change of direction greater than 45Â° and at the property boundary.

6. Common drainage problems in African homes and how to fix them

  • Recurring WC blockages: usually a flat or back-falling 110 mm run, or a builder's rubble/debris left in the pipe. Fix: re-grade to 1:50, rod and camera the line, and flush.
  • Sewer smell in bathrooms: dry P-trap from an unvented or siphoned branch, or a missing gully trap. Fix: add a vent and refill/repair the trap seal.
  • Slow shower and basin drainage: hair and soap in the trap, or undersized 40 mm branch on a long run. Fix: clean the trap; upgrade the branch to 50 mm.
  • Septic tank overflowing after heavy rain: soakaway undersized or groundwater ingress. Fix: increase soakaway area, and check that surface water is not draining into the tank.
  • Joint leaks at couplings: solvent cement applied to wet pipe, or a mismatched rubber ring. Fix: cut out and re-make the joint dry, with the correct cement and cleaner.
  • Roots in the drain: cracked pipe at a joint. Fix: replace the section and re-bed with compacted sand surround.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the receiving point (sewer invert level or septic tank position) before ordering pipe.
  2. Size each branch to the fixture table: WC 110 mm, shower/basin/sink 50 mm minimum.
  3. Set the main drain at 1:50 (within the 1:60â1:40 band) and check with a level every 5 m.
  4. Fit one P-trap per fixture with a 50â75 mm water seal; never double-trap.
  5. Vent within 1.5 m of each trap; terminate the stack 150 mm above the roof, clear of windows.
  6. Install an inspection chamber or rodding eye at every bend over 45Â° and at the boundary.
  7. Solvent-weld only dry, clean pipe ends; allow full cure before pressure/flow testing.
  8. Pressure/water-test the line before backfilling, and photograph the layout for the client file.

Further Reading (free, official)

  • British Standards Institution â BS EN 12056-2:2000, Gravity drainage systems inside buildings: Sanitary pipework, layout and calculation. bsigroup.com
  • International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials (IAPMO) â Uniform Plumbing Code, Chapter 7 Sanitary Drainage. iapmo.org
  • South African Government â National Building Regulations, Part P: Drainage. gov.za
  • World Health Organization â Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater (Vol. 1â4, free PDF). who.int
  • UN-Habitat â Sanitation and Wastewater Management in African Cities (free reports). unhabitat.org

Prepared as a practical reference for the Rise Africa Skills â PVC & Plumbing Pipes course. Always verify dimensions, gradients and permit requirements against your national building code and local utility before quoting or installing.

quiz.q: What are the three main functions of a DWV system?
options: A) Drain wastewater, carry solid waste, vent sewer gases
B) Supply water, heat water, filter water
C) Store water, pump water, treat water
D) Irrigate gardens, fill pools, wash cars
quiz.explanation: DWV stands for Drain, Waste, and Vent, which are its three core functions.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended diameter for a toilet drain pipe?
quiz.explanation: Toilets discharge solid waste and need a 110 mm (4-inch) pipe to prevent clogs.

quiz.q: What is the correct slope range for horizontal drainage pipes?
quiz.explanation: The standard slope for PVC drainage is between 1:60 and 1:40 to balance flow and solid transport.

quiz.q: Why is a P-trap used under sinks and showers?
options: B) To hold a water seal that blocks sewer gas
C) To filter out food particles
quiz.explanation: The water in the P-trap creates a seal that prevents sewer gases from entering the home.

quiz.q: Where should a vent pipe terminate?
options: C) At least 300 mm above the roof
quiz.explanation: Vent pipes must extend above the roof to safely release gases and allow air into the system.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pipe diameter for a kitchen sink drain?
quiz.explanation: 40 mm (1.5-inch) pipe is standard for sinks, though 50 mm is better for long runs.

quiz.q: How much drop should a 5-metre drain pipe have at a 1:60 slope?
quiz.explanation: At 1:60, 5 metres (500 cm) divided by 60 gives approximately 8.3 cm drop.

quiz.q: What tool is used to clear a clogged toilet?
quiz.explanation: A plunger, toilet auger, or drain snake can all be used, depending on the severity of the clog.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using caustic soda in PVC pipes?
options: B) It can soften and damage the PVC
D) It freezes in cold weather
quiz.explanation: Caustic soda generates heat and can soften PVC, leading to deformation or leaks.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of bad smells from drains?
options: A) Too much water in the trap
B) A dry trap or blocked vent
quiz.explanation: A dry trap allows gas through, and a blocked vent prevents proper air flow, causing odors.

quiz.q: How often should a septic tank be pumped out?
quiz.explanation: Regular pumping every 2â3 years prevents solids from overflowing into the drain field.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cleanout in a drainage system?
options: B) To allow access for rodding clogs
quiz.explanation: A cleanout is a capped fitting that provides access to rod or snake the drain line.

quiz.q: What should you do if tree roots have entered a drain pipe?
options: B) Cut out the damaged section and replace with new PVC
quiz.explanation: Roots must be physically removed, and the damaged pipe section replaced to prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended length for a 40 mm trap arm?
quiz.explanation: A 40 mm trap arm should not exceed 1.5 m to prevent siphonage of the trap seal.

quiz.q: What is an air admittance valve (AAV)?
options: A) A device that lets air into the drain without a roof vent
B) A type of pipe cement
quiz.explanation: An AAV is a one-way valve that admits air when needed, often used when roof venting is not possible.

quiz.q: Why should you never connect stormwater to a septic tank?
options: B) It overloads the tank and kills bacteria
quiz.explanation: Stormwater adds excess water, flushing out bacteria and causing the tank to overflow.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pipe diameter for a main drain from house to septic tank?
quiz.explanation: 110 mm is the minimum standard for main drain lines to handle solids and flow.

quiz.q: What causes gurgling sounds in drains?
options: B) A blocked or undersized vent
quiz.explanation: Gurgling indicates air is being pulled through the trap due to a venting problem.

quiz.q: What should you do if a floor drain overflows?
options: A) Remove the grate and clean the trap
quiz.explanation: Overflow is often due to a clogged trap; removing the grate allows you to clear it.

quiz.q: How can you prevent trap seal evaporation in dry season?
options: A) Add cooking oil to the trap
quiz.explanation: A thin layer of cooking oil slows evaporation, keeping the water seal intact.

quiz.q: What is the correct slope for a horizontal vent pipe?
quiz.explanation: Horizontal vent pipes should slope back to the drain at 1:60 to allow condensate to drain.

quiz.q: What is a backwater valve used for?
options: A) To prevent sewage from backing up into the house
quiz.explanation: A backwater valve closes when sewage flows backward, protecting the home from flooding.

quiz.q: What is the minimum water depth required in a P-trap?
quiz.explanation: A water seal of at least 50 mm is needed to effectively block sewer gases.

quiz.q: Which fitting is best for changing direction in a drain line to reduce clogs?
quiz.explanation: Two 45-degree bends create a gentler turn than a 90-degree elbow, reducing clog risk.

quiz.q: What should you do before connecting to a municipal sewer?
options: A) Obtain permission from local council
quiz.explanation: Connecting to public sewers often requires permission and may need a licensed plumber.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a septic tank is full?
options: B) Green grass over the drain field
C) Sewage smell in the house
quiz.explanation: All these are common signs that a septic tank needs pumping.

quiz.q: How often should you add water to a septic tank?
quiz.explanation: Adding a bucket of water monthly helps maintain bacterial activity and prevents drying.

quiz.q: What is the best way to cut PVC pipe?
options: A) Fine-tooth saw or pipe cutter
quiz.explanation: A fine-tooth saw or pipe cutter gives a clean, square cut that ensures proper gluing.

quiz.q: What should you apply to PVC before solvent cement?
quiz.explanation: Primer cleans and softens the PVC surface, ensuring a strong solvent weld.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of slow drains in African homes?
options: A) Hair, soap, and food clogs
quiz.explanation: Accumulated hair, soap scum, and food particles are the most frequent culprits.
